title: Two boons, and no third
hook: the question is never answered, but omens frighten the blind king, and Draupadi frees her husbands with two boons
carry: lobha: wanting without end wears dharma away
tomorrow: Why go back for one more game?

segments.voice: Yesterday Vidura told of Prahlada, and still no one answered Draupadi. Elders who won't speak dharma aren't elders.

Draupadi asks one more time. In the telling, she says she has been dragged here and wronged before everyone, and still no one has spoken. Then, once more: am I a slave, or free? Say it, and I'll accept it. And this time something does answer, though not from the people in the hall. By the end of this long day, a blind king finally speaks.

Bhishma answers once more, and again he can't settle it: Yudhishthira alone, he says, should say whether she was won. Duryodhana, smiling, sets a trap: let the four younger brothers say Yudhishthira wasn't their master, and she'll be free. Before they answer, Duryodhana makes an insulting gesture toward Draupadi, and Bhima swears a second vow, against him. Arjuna answers the trap: he was our master when he staked us, but whose master was he once he'd lost himself? Then the sounds begin. A jackal howls in the chamber where the king's sacred fire is kept. Donkeys bray. Birds cry out. Gandhari and Vidura hear it and tell the blind king. And Dhritarashtra, frightened, finally acts. He rebukes his son and offers Draupadi a boon. She asks for Yudhishthira's freedom, so her son won't be called a slave's son. Granted. A second: that the other four go free, with their weapons and chariots. Granted. Then he offers a third, and Draupadi refuses. Greed, she says, wears away dharma. A woman of a warrior's house may ask two boons; her husbands, now free, can win the rest by their own deeds. That word is lobha, greed, and Hindu teaching counts it among the six inner enemies, beside desire and anger. Notice: asking wasn't the problem. Draupadi asked, and asked well, for exactly what freed the people she loved. Lobha is the wanting that never stops. She knew where enough was, and put the asking down.
screen: `DURYODHANA SETS A TRAP.` · `ARJUNA: WHOSE MASTER WAS HE?` · `THE BLIND KING OFFERS A BOON.` · `GREED WEARS AWAY DHARMA.` · then, large: `SHE KNEW WHERE ENOUGH WAS.`

segments.voice: Many Hindus begin their own requests with a prayer for everyone: sarve bhavantu sukhinah, may all be happy, may all be free from illness. Say it, or its meaning. Then ask for one or two things you truly need, and stop there, the way Draupadi did. If you pray, offer the rest to God; if you don't, notice what it feels like to want enough.
Draupadi's question. Never answered by the hall, yet by the day's end she asks two boons, frees five brothers, and refuses a third.
Your line: lobha: wanting without end wears dharma away. Two boons, and no third. Day seven hundred seventy-five, done.

howItsDone: Draupadi's two boons and her refusal of a third are retold as a picture of dignity and of lobha, greed, refused; in parts of south India Draupadi herself is honored as a goddess.

lobha.meaning: greed; one of the six inner enemies

Confirm the omens (jackal howling in the homa chamber of Dhritarashtra, asses braying, birds crying) and that Gandhari and Vidura report them to the king.
Confirm Draupadi's boons and her stated reason (her son Prativindhya should not be called a slave's son), and her refusal of the third (a kshatriya woman may ask two).
